core: What causation means in history: explaining why events happened, not just when
Multiple causation: major events have many interacting causes, not a single one
Ranking causes by importance and how that ranking depends on interpretation
Long-term / underlying causes versus short-term / immediate causes and triggers (sparks)
Correlation and sequence in time are not proof of causation (post hoc reasoning)
Contingency: outcomes were not inevitable; events could have unfolded differently
supporting: The classic textbook structure of layered war causes illustrated with an accurately dated example (World War I, 1914)
How ranking causes links causation to interpretation

Historical context as a standalone skill (sibling topic)

claims.claim: Causation in history is the search for why events happened and what brought them about; historians rank causes because not all causes are equally significant.
Major historical events almost always result from multiple interacting causes rather than a single monocausal explanation; standards explicitly warn against simple, monocausal explanations.

Historians distinguish long-term / underlying circumstances from immediate causes; how important each cause is judged to be depends on the historian's interpretive framework, so historians often disagree about ranking even when the facts are clear.

Contingency is the idea that historical outcomes were not preordained or inevitable and could have unfolded differently depending on choices and circumstances; historical thinking challenges arguments of inevitability by formulating examples of contingency.

One event preceding another in time does not by itself prove the first caused the second; historians distinguish coincidence and correlation from causation, and treat causal explanations as informed hypotheses grounded in evidence rather than unsupported opinion.

Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914; Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914, and by early August 1914 the alliance systems had drawn Europe's major powers into the First World War. The war is conventionally explained by long-term factors (militarism, alliance systems, imperial rivalry, nationalism) plus the assassination as an immediate trigger.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How to rank the causes of World War I (e.g., how much weight to give German policy, alliance systems, or nationalism).
positions: Historians continue to debate which underlying causes were most decisive and how much responsibility to assign to particular states.
There is broad agreement on the facts and sequence of events in 1914 even where interpretations of importance differ.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses World War I only to illustrate the generic structure of layered causes and an immediate trigger, and explicitly notes that ranking the causes is an interpretive question historians still debate. It does not assert a single 'real cause' or assign blame.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft was generic boilerplate ('Causation is a foundational concept in History... this lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it') with no substantive, sourced content. Its wording was discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with sourced treatment of multiple causation, long/short-term causes and triggers, correlation vs causation, contingency, and cause vs consequence.
Added an accurately dated World War I example with dates verified against Library of Congress and Britannica.

sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 1, to 1500 — 1.3 Causation and Interpretation in History
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed OER survey text. Supports: causation is the 'why' behind events; not all causes are equally significant so historians rank them; immediate vs long-term circumstances; a layered (primary/secondary/tertiary) framing of causes; and that ranking causes depends on the historian's interpretation, so historians disagree even when facts are clear. Facts synthesized; prose written originally, no source wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Historical Thinking Standards — Standard 3: Historical Analysis and Interpretation
sourceRecords.provider: National Center for History in the Schools, UCLA (Public History Initiative)
sourceRecords.notes: Widely used U.S. history-education standards. Supports: analyze cause-and-effect bearing in mind multiple causation (individuals, ideas/interests/beliefs, and the role of chance and the accidental); avoid simple monocausal explanations and arguments of inevitability; challenge inevitability by formulating examples of historical contingency; and distinguish unsupported opinion from informed, evidence-grounded hypotheses. © UCLA; used REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: Contingency (Ask a Master Teacher)
sourceRecords.provider: TeachingHistory.org — Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media, George Mason University (U.S. Dept. of Education funded)
sourceRecords.notes: History-education resource. Supports the definition of contingency as the opposite of inevitability: historic events and trends result from a variety of factors coming together and are not preordained or unavoidable, so outcomes could have unfolded differently. Used REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand: Topics in Chronicling America
sourceRecords.notes: Library of Congress research guide.
